# Kaposi sarcoma

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Opportunistic infections > Kaposi sarcoma*

[Original Article Link](/library/BH0zsh)

---

## Summary

Kaposi <u>sarcoma</u> is a malignant, multifocal, highly vascularized <u>tumor</u> of the <u>endothelial</u> cells that most commonly affects the <u>skin</u> but may also involve the <u>lymph nodes</u>, <u>mucosa</u>, and <u>viscera</u>. It is commonly associated with <u>HIV</u> and can occur at any <u>CD4 count</u> (typically < 500/mmÂ³). Diagnosis is confirmed with <u>biopsy</u>. Treatment depends on whether the disease is localized or disseminated; all patients with <u>HIV</u> should be started on <u>ART</u>.

---

## Etiology

* Caused by <u>human herpesvirus 8</u> (<u>HHV8</u>), a large <u>DNA</u> <u>gamma herpes virus</u>

* Routes of transmission include [[2]](/library/05XeiA)

* Saliva

* Sexual contact

* Potentially via <u>blood transfusion</u> and IV drug use

---

## Clinical features

Patients typically present with multiple cutaneous or <u>visceral</u> elevated tumors with rapid growth. [[2]](/library/05XeiA)[[3]](/library/GtXBU-)




* Most commonly affects the <u>skin</u> but may also involve the <u>lymph nodes</u>, <u>mucosa</u>, and <u>viscera</u>

* Can occur at any <u>CD4 count</u>;  (typically < 500/mmÂ³)





* Initial stage: 

* Painless, nonpruritic, violet <u>papules</u> or <u>nodules</u> on <u>skin</u> and <u>mucosa</u> (especially face/<u>oral cavity</u> and chest)

* Solitary, darkly pigmented <u>plaques</u>, which can evolve into nodular, bluish, <u>submucosal</u>, and painful <u>skin</u> changes

* Lesions resemble those of <u>bacillary angiomatosis</u>.

* Progression: may disseminate to the organs, particularly the <u>gastrointestinal tract</u>, respiratory tract, and <u>lymph nodes</u>.

* <u>Gastrointestinal tract</u> involvement: abdominal <u>pain</u> and <u>diarrhea</u>; hemorrhage and <u>bowel obstruction</u> in severe cases

* Pulmonary involvement: Lesions cause <u>dyspnea</u>, <u>cough</u>, and/or <u>hemoptysis</u>.

> [!TIP]
> Cutaneous lesions are the typical initial manifestation of KS. However, extracutaneous lesions (disseminated disease) can precede <u>skin</u> involvement. [[4]](/library/7FX4j-)




> [!TIP]
> Lesions resemble those of <u>bacillary angiomatosis</u> and <u>histology</u> is required to differentiate between the conditions.

---

## Subtypes and variants

* HIV/AIDS-associated KS (<u>epidemic KS</u>):

* Most common <u>HIV</u>-associated <u>tumor</u> disease

* Commonly manifests as multiple cutaneous lesions on the face, limbs, and torso

* Classic KS; : usually occurs in older Mediterranean or Eastern European men

* Iatrogenic KS; : usually occurs in <u>immunosuppressed</u> patients after organ transplants

* Endemic KS

* Most commonly occurs in Sub-Saharan Africa in <u>HIV</u>-uninfected individuals

* Aggressive disease with <u>lymph node</u> and <u>visceral</u> involvement is common in children





References: [[2]](/library/05XeiA)[[3]](/library/GtXBU-)[[5]](/library/ttXX2-)

---

## Diagnosis

* <u>HIV screening</u>

* <u>Biopsy</u> and <u>histology</u> of cutaneous or <u>visceral</u> lesions (indicated in all patients)

* <u>Spindle shaped cells</u>, <u>leukocyte</u> infiltration, and <u>angiogenesis</u>

* <u>Immunostaining</u>  helps differentiate KS from other similar diagnoses (e.g., <u>bacillary angiomatosis</u>)

* CT with IV contrast: contrast-<u>enhancement</u> of lesions  [[6]](/library/sFXtj-)

* Chest: diffuse reticulonodular infiltrates, <u>pleural effusion</u>, peribronchovascular <u>nodules</u>

* Abdomen/<u>pelvis</u>: <u>hepatomegaly</u>, multifocal <u>liver</u> <u>nodules</u> with contrast-<u>enhancement</u>, bowel wall thickening, <u>lymphadenopathy</u>

* Lytic bony lesions and <u>soft tissue</u> masses may also be seen.

* Additional studies (depending on symptoms): Endoscopy and <u>bronchoscopy</u> may show red-purple lesions; hemorrhage may also be visible.





References: [[2]](/library/05XeiA)[[3]](/library/GtXBU-)[[5]](/library/ttXX2-)

---

## Treatment

The decision to treat depends on whether the disease is localized or disseminated, as well as whether there is any underlying <u>immunosuppression</u>.




* <u>Immunosuppressed</u> patients: Manage underlying <u>immunosuppression</u> (first-line treatment).

* <u>HIV-associated KS</u>: Start <u>ART</u>. [[2]](/library/05XeiA)

* <u>Chemotherapy</u> (liposomal <u>doxorubicin</u> and <u>paclitaxel</u>): indicated for systemic disease; consider for disseminated cutaneous disease.

* If feasible, reduce doses of, or change, <u>immunosuppressive</u> medications.

* Immunocompetent patients or inadequate response to first-line therapy for <u>immunosuppressed</u> patients

* Localized disease: intralesional <u>chemotherapy</u> , <u>cryotherapy</u>, <u>radiation therapy</u>, or laser therapy

* Systemic disease

* Systemic <u>chemotherapy</u> with liposomal <u>anthracyclines</u> or <u>paclitaxel</u>

* α-<u>interferon</u>





References: [[2]](/library/05XeiA)[[3]](/library/GtXBU-)[[5]](/library/ttXX2-)
